objectives.text: Given a simple electrical circuit, APPLY basic electrical theory fundamental principles to describe circuit operation.

enabling.text: DESCRIBE the following electrical parameters, including the unit of measurement and the relationship to other parameters.

enabling.text: Given a standard electrical symbol, IDENTIFY the component that the symbol represents. The symbols will be for the following components:

passages.quote: This attraction is called electrostatic force, the force that holds the electron in orbit.
unlike charges (like electrons and protons) attract each other, and like charges repel each other.
Forces of this type are the result of an electrostatic field that exists around each charged particle or object.
Potential difference is the term used to describe how large the electrostatic force is between two charged objects.
The sum of the potential differences of all charged particles in the electrostatic field is referred to as electromotive force (EMF).
If the atom loses one or more electrons, it becomes positively charged and is referred to as a positive ion.
Conductors are materials with electrons that are loosely bound to their atoms, or materials that permit free motion of a large number of electrons.
Insulators, or nonconductors, are materials with electrons that are tightly bound to their atoms and require large amounts of energy to free them from the influence of the nucleus.
Resistors are made of materials that conduct electricity, but offer opposition to current flow.
This flow of positive charges is known as conventional current
A direct current flows continuously in the same direction.
An alternating current periodically reverses direction.
An ideal source is a theoretical concept of an electric current or voltage supply (such as a battery) that has no losses and is a perfect voltage or current supply.
A real source is a real life current or voltage supply that has some losses associated with it.
Resistance is defined as the opposition to current flow.
Applied voltage equals circuit current times the circuit resistance.
If any two of the component values are known, the third can be calculated.
Conductance is found by taking the reciprocal of the resistance.
power is the rate at which work is done, or the rate at which heat is generated.
power can be described as the current (I) in a circuit squared times the resistance (R) of the circuit.
Inductance is defined as the ability of a coil to store energy, induce a voltage in itself, and oppose changes in current flowing through it.
Capacitance is defined as the ability to store an electric charge
A generator is a machine that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by using the principle of magnetic induction.
This generation of voltage is known as the piezoelectric effect.
This process is called thermoelectricity.
This phenomenon is called the photoelectric effect
The liberation of electrons from a hot surface is called thermionic emission.
The group of magnetic field lines emitted outward from the north pole of a magnet is called magnetic flux.
Magnetic flux density is the amount of magnetic flux per unit area of a section, perpendicular to the direction of flux.
Permeability (µ) refers to the ability of a material to concentrate magnetic lines of flux.
These materials have a relative permeability of slightly more than one.
These materials have a relative permeability of less than one.
Magnetomotive force (mmf) is the strength of a magnetic field in a coil of wire.
Opposition to the production of flux in a material is called reluctance, which corresponds to resistance.
The mmf can be compared with EMF, and the flux (Φ) can be compared to current.
magnetic flux (Φ) is proportional to the magnetomotive force (Fm)
The BH Magnetization Curve (Figure 27) shows how much flux density (B) results from increasing the flux intensity (H).
The magnetic flux in an iron core lags behind the magnetizing force.
The greater the area inside the hysteresis loop, the larger the hysteresis losses.
there must be relative motion between the conductor and the magnetic lines of force in order to induce an EMF.
The magnitude of the induced voltage depends on two factors: (1) the number of turns of a coil, and (2) how fast the conductor cuts across the magnetic lines of force, or flux.
Induced voltage has a polarity that will oppose the change causing the induction.
The symbols for the various electrical components that will appear on electrical diagrams and schematics are shown in Figure 30.

body.text: An atom consists of a positively charged nucleus surrounded by negatively charged electrons, so the atom as a whole is electrically neutral.
These facts are known as the First Law of Electrostatics.
The strength of the attraction or repulsion depends on the amount of charge on each object and the distance between them.

body.cap: Potential Difference Between Two Charged Objects
body.alt: Lines of force between a negatively charged object and a positively charged object, with an electron pushed toward the positive object.

body.text: The basic unit of measure of potential difference is the volt, so potential difference is also called voltage.
The electrons in the outermost shell are called valence electrons. Enough applied energy makes some of them leave the atom, and these are free electrons.
If an atom gains one or more electrons, it becomes negatively charged and is referred to as a negative ion.

checks.q: What force holds an electron in orbit around a nucleus?
checks.x: The attraction between the electron and the nucleus is called electrostatic force, the force that holds the electron in orbit.

checks.q: An atom loses one electron. What does it become?
checks.x: If the atom loses one or more electrons, it becomes positively charged and is referred to as a positive ion.

body.text: Copper, silver, and gold are examples of good conductors. Most metals are good conductors.
Examples of insulators are rubber, plastics, glass, and dry wood.
Electron flow is from a point of negative potential to a point of positive potential.

body.cap: Potential Difference Across a Conductor Causes a Current to Flow
body.alt: A battery connected across a conductor, with a solid arrow for electron flow and a dashed arrow for conventional current in the opposite direction.

body.text: Both conventions are in use and they are essentially equivalent. This handbook uses electron flow.
Ideal sources are used for analytical purposes only, since they cannot occur in nature.

checks.q: Which material has electrons that are loosely bound to its atoms?
checks.x: Conductors are materials with electrons that are loosely bound to their atoms.

checks.q: Why are ideal sources used for analytical purposes only?
checks.x: An ideal source is a theoretical concept with no losses, so it is used for analysis only.

body.text: Voltage is the pressure or force that causes electrons to move in a conductor. It is measured in volts and written as E in equations.
Current is the movement of free electrons through a conductor. It is measured in amperes and written as I. One ampere is one coulomb of charge moving past a given point in one second.
Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω) and written as R. One ohm limits the current to one ampere when one volt is applied.
E = IR
G = 1/R
The unit of conductance is the mho, which is ohm spelled backwards.
Electric power is measured in watts.
P = I x E   or   P = I²R
Inductance (L) is measured in henries. One henry permits one volt to be induced when the current through the coil changes at one ampere per second.
Capacitance (C) is measured in farads. It equals the charge stored divided by the voltage applied.

checks.q: In what unit is capacitance measured?
checks.x: Capacitance is measured in farads. Henries measure inductance, mhos measure conductance, and webers measure magnetic flux.

checks.q: A 4 ohm resistor has what conductance?
checks.x: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance: G = 1/R = 1/4 = 0.25 mho.

checks.q: A current of 2 amps flows through 10 ohms. Using P = I²R, what is the power?
checks.x: P = I²R = (2)²(10) = 40 watts.

checks.q: A circuit has 24 volts applied across 6 ohms. What current flows?
checks.x: By Ohm's Law, I = E/R = 24/6 = 4 amps.

body.text: Electrochemistry: a chemical reaction produces and maintains opposite charges on two dissimilar metals in contact with an electrolyte solution, as in the voltaic chemical cell.
Static electricity: removing electrons from a body, as happens due to friction, leaves it with an unequal charge, and an electric force is exerted between it and a body with a normal charge.
Magnetic induction produces a voltage by rotating coils of wire through a stationary magnetic field, or by rotating a magnetic field through stationary coils of wire.

body.alt: A coil rotating between north and south magnet poles, connected to a load, showing the direction of motion and the field.

body.text: Pressure on certain crystals or ceramics drives electrons out of orbit in the direction of the force, building up opposite charges on opposite sides.
When two dissimilar metals are joined and heat is applied to the junction, electrons transfer between them and a voltage appears across the junction.
When photons in a light beam strike a material, the energy transfer may dislodge electrons from their orbits, leaving the material positively charged.
At sufficiently high temperatures, a considerable number of electrons are able to escape from a hot cathode.

checks.q: Heating the junction of two dissimilar metals produces a voltage. What is this process called?
checks.x: Heat applied to the junction of two dissimilar metals produces a voltage. This process is called thermoelectricity.

checks.q: Which method produces a voltage by applying pressure to certain crystals?
checks.x: Applying pressure to certain crystals drives electrons out of orbit. This generation of voltage is known as the piezoelectric effect.

body.text: The law of magnetism states that like magnetic poles repel and unlike magnetic poles attract one another.
The SI unit of magnetic flux is the weber (Wb). One weber is equal to 1 x 10⁸ magnetic field lines.
B = Φ / A
B is flux density in teslas, Φ is flux in webers, and A is area in square meters.
Relative permeability is the ratio of the permeability of a material to the permeability of a vacuum.
Ferromagnetic materials include iron, steel, nickel, cobalt, and the commercial alloys alnico and peralloy.
Paramagnetic materials include aluminum, platinum, manganese, and chromium.
Diamagnetic materials include bismuth, antimony, copper, zinc, mercury, gold, and silver.
An electric current flowing through a conductor produces a magnetic field around that conductor. The left-hand rule relates the current flow to the direction of the magnetic lines of force.

body.cap: Left-hand Rule for Current Carrying Conductors
body.alt: A left hand gripping a conductor, with the thumb in the direction of current flow and the fingers around the conductor showing the direction of the magnetic field.

body.text: Fm = ampere-turns = NI
Field intensity depends on the length of the coil: H = NI / L, in ampere-turns per meter.
Reluctance is inversely proportional to permeability. Iron cores have high permeability and low reluctance. Air has low permeability and high reluctance.

checks.q: What is opposition to the production of flux in a material called?
checks.x: Opposition to the production of flux in a material is called reluctance, which corresponds to resistance.

checks.q: A coil has 200 turns and carries 3 amps. What is its magnetomotive force?
checks.x: Fm = NI = (200)(3) = 600 ampere-turns.

checks.q: Which group of materials has a relative permeability of less than one?
checks.x: Diamagnetic materials, such as bismuth, copper, and silver, have a relative permeability of less than one.

body.text: A magnetic circuit can be compared with an electric circuit. The mmf can be compared with EMF, and the flux can be compared to current.
Φ = Fm / R
Reluctance is found from the length of the coil, the permeability of the magnetic material, and the cross-sectional area of the coil.

body.cap: Typical BH Curve for Two Types of Soft Iron
body.alt: Graph of flux density B against flux intensity H for two soft irons and air. Each iron curve rises steeply, then flattens at a knee.

body.text: Flux density increases rapidly with flux intensity before the core saturates, or develops a knee. After that, an increase in flux intensity has little or no effect on flux density.
When current in a coil reverses direction thousands of times per second, hysteresis can cause considerable loss of energy.

body.alt: Hysteresis loop of flux density B against field H, reaching plus and minus Bmax, crossing the B axis at Br and the H axis at Hc.

body.text: Retentivity is the flux density remaining after the magnetizing force is zero. Coercive force is the force that must be applied in the reverse direction to reduce flux density to zero.

checks.q: In a magnetic circuit, which quantity is compared to current in an electric circuit?
checks.x: The mmf can be compared with EMF, and the flux can be compared to current.

checks.q: A coil has an mmf of 900 At and a reluctance of 3 x 10⁶ At/Wb. What is the flux?
checks.x: Flux equals mmf divided by reluctance: 900 / (3 x 10⁶) = 300 x 10⁻⁶ Wb, or 300 µWb.

checks.q: On a BH curve, what happens to flux density after the knee?
o: It changes little or not at all as H increases
checks.x: Once the core saturates at the knee, an increase in flux intensity H has little or no effect on flux density B.

checks.q: What does a larger area inside the hysteresis loop mean?
checks.x: The greater the area inside the hysteresis loop, the larger the hysteresis losses.

body.text: If a conductor cuts across lines of magnetic force, or if magnetic lines of force cut across a conductor, a voltage is induced into the conductor.

body.alt: A conductor moved through three positions between magnet poles, connected to a galvanometer that detects the induced voltage.

body.text: Vind = -N (ΔΦ / Δt)
N is the number of turns in the coil, and ΔΦ/Δt is the rate at which the flux cuts across the conductor.
The negative sign in the equation shows that the induced voltage acts to oppose the change.

checks.q: A coil is stationary in a flux that stays constant. What voltage is induced?
o: A voltage equal to the number of turns
checks.x: There must be relative motion between the conductor and the magnetic lines of force in order to induce an EMF.

checks.q: The flux through a 10 turn coil changes by 6 Wb in 2 seconds. What is the magnitude of the induced voltage?
checks.x: Vind = N(ΔΦ/Δt) = (10)(6/2) = 30 volts in magnitude.

checks.q: What does Lenz's Law state about induced voltage?
o: Its polarity opposes the change causing the induction
It always aids the change causing the induction
It does not depend on motion
checks.x: Induced voltage has a polarity that will oppose the change causing the induction.

facts.q: State the First Law of Electrostatics.
facts.a: Unlike charges attract each other, and like charges repel each other.
The sum of the potential differences of all charged particles in the electrostatic field.

facts.q: State the three ways to write Ohm's Law from E, I, and R.
facts.a: E = IR, I = E/R, and R = E/I. If any two of the values are known, the third can be calculated.
The group of magnetic field lines emitted outward from the north pole of a magnet.
The ability of a material to concentrate magnetic lines of flux.

facts.q: What two factors set the magnitude of an induced voltage?
facts.a: The number of turns of a coil, and how fast the conductor cuts across the magnetic lines of force, or flux.

summary.text: Electrostatic force holds an electron in orbit around a nucleus, and potential difference measures how large that force is between two charged objects.
Conductors have electrons loosely bound to their atoms, and insulators have electrons tightly bound to their atoms.
Voltage is measured in volts, resistance in ohms, conductance in mhos, power in watts, inductance in henries, and capacitance in farads.
Voltage can be produced by electrochemistry, static electricity, magnetic induction, the piezoelectric effect, thermoelectricity, the photoelectric effect, and thermionic emission.
Reluctance is the opposition to the production of flux in a material.
A BH curve shows how much flux density results from increasing flux intensity, and the knee marks where further increases have minimal effect.
Faraday's Law: induced voltage depends on the number of turns of a coil and how fast the conductor cuts the flux. Lenz's Law: an induced voltage opposes the change that caused it.

blend_notes.note: The flux density example states the area as 0.004 m², then solves with 0.0004 m². The example is not used.

The text gives relative permeabilities of 50 to 200 for ferrites only, but the summary on p.36 gives that range for all ferromagnetic materials. Objective 1.7 asks for an approximate value, so the lesson leaves the range out for ferromagnetic materials.
The text says static electricity acts when a body comes near but not in contact with another, while the summary on p.26 says it comes in contact. The lesson uses neither phrase.
Page 8 prints "ion change" where objective 1.1 says ion charge. The lesson uses positive ion and negative ion.
